stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: Why does "cake" have a long a sound but "cap" a short one? What does the final e do?
explain: Many English words follow spelling patterns. A silent e at the end often makes the vowel say its name: cap becomes cape, hop becomes hope, kit becomes kite.
Some letters work as a team. Sh, ch and th make new sounds, and ee and ai make long vowel sounds. Learning these teams helps you read new words.
stages.mnemonic: Magic e: it does not talk, but it makes the vowel shout its name.
items: a small hat with a front
a sweet food baked in an oven
a farm animal that gives wool
sentences: The sheep sleep in the field.

gq.q: What does the silent e do in "kite"?
o: It makes the i say its name
It makes the vowel sound shorter and quicker
gq.why: The final e signals a long vowel: kit versus kite.

gq.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as "rain"?
gq.why: Ai in rain and a-e in plane both make the long a sound.

panel.q: Why is "knife" spelled with a k you do not hear?
o: Old English had a /k/ sound that was lost in speech but kept in spelling
English letters are chosen at random
The k makes the i long
The k is for American spelling only
panel.why: Many silent letters (knee, knight) were pronounced centuries ago; spelling stayed while sound changed.

panel.q: Which word is NOT regular for the magic-e rule?
panel.why: Have has a short a sound despite the final e.

panel.q: Why is "though" hard to read for learners?
panel.model: The letters ough stand for different sounds in though, through, tough and cough, so spelling does not predict sound.
panel.why: English spelling is not fully regular.

teach.topic: How silent e changes a word
teach.model: At the end of many words, e is silent. It makes the vowel before it say its name. So cap becomes cape and kit becomes kite.

points.ask: What does the last e do?
Can you show me a pair?

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: "Dog the barks" sounds wrong, but "The dog barks" sounds right. What is the rule?
explain: A simple English sentence has a subject, then a verb, then often an object: "Maya eats rice." The subject does the action. The order is very important in English.
Adjectives come before nouns and adverbs often come after verbs. To make a negative sentence, use do not (don't) or does not (doesn't) before the verb: "She doesn't eat fish."
stages.mnemonic: Who? Does what? To what? Subject, Verb, Object: S-V-O.
items: the person who does the action
the thing that receives the action
a sentence that ends with a full stop
a group of words with a full thought

gq.q: Which sentence has the correct word order?
gq.why: English normally uses subject, verb, object.

gq.q: How do you make "He plays football" negative?
gq.why: After does not, the verb is in its base form: play.

panel.q: "The dog bites the man" and "The man bites the dog" differ in meaning because...
o: word order shows who does the action
the nouns have different endings in each sentence
panel.why: English has little case marking, so position shows who is the subject and who is the object.

panel.q: Why is "She not like fish" wrong, and how do you correct it?
panel.model: English negatives need the helper does/doesn't, then the base verb: She does not like fish.
panel.why: Negation with do-support.

panel.q: Which sentence is a complete sentence?
panel.why: It has a subject and a verb and expresses a full idea.

teach.topic: How to build a simple English sentence
teach.model: Put the doer first, then the action, then what it acts on: Maya eats rice. To make it negative add does not before the verb for he, she and it.

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: Why do we say "I went" and not "I goed"? Some verbs break the rules.
explain: Most English verbs add -ed for the past: walk, walked. These are regular verbs. Some very common verbs are irregular and change in other ways: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw.
The past tense is the same for all people, so I went, she went and they went. For a present habit use the plain form, and add -s for he, she or it.
stages.mnemonic: Regular verbs add -ed. Irregular verbs sneak away in a new form.

gq.q: What is the past tense of "go"?
gq.why: Go is irregular: go, went, gone.

panel.q: Why do children say "I goed"?
o: They apply the regular -ed rule to an irregular verb
They have not heard the word went
panel.why: This overgeneralisation shows children learn rules.

panel.q: What is the difference between "went" and "gone"?
o: went is simple past; gone is the participle after have
they are the same word in two spellings
gone is the simple past; went is the participle used after have
panel.why: We say I went, but I have gone.

panel.q: How can you learn irregular verbs?
panel.model: Practise them in sentences and review lists often, because their forms must be remembered.
panel.why: Irregular forms are learned by use.

teach.model: To talk about the past, most verbs add -ed, like walked. Some verbs are irregular. Go becomes went and eat becomes ate, so you have to remember them.

points.ask: How do regular verbs make the past?

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
stages.hook: "Tom is happy. He is kind." Who is "He"? Words that stand for nouns save time.
explain: A pronoun stands in for a noun: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object forms are me, you, him, her, it, us, them. "Give it to me" uses object forms.
Modifiers add detail. Adjectives describe nouns (a tall tree). Possessives show who owns something: my, your, his, her, our, their. Use a, an or the before nouns.
stages.mnemonic: I do it. It is done to me. Subject I, object me.
items: a word for a boy or man
a word for a girl or woman
a word for more than one person (not you)
the form of I after a verb

gq.q: Choose the correct word: "Give the pen to ___."
gq.why: After to, we use the object form me.
Their is the possessive form of they.

panel.q: Which is correct?
panel.why: Their shows possession, there shows place, and they're means they are.

panel.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: My friend and I went home.
Me and my friend went home.
My friend and me went home.
I and my friend went home.
panel.why: In careful English, the subject form I is used, and it is polite to name the other person first.

panel.q: Why do we say "I like him" and not "I like he"?
panel.model: Pronouns change form: he is the subject form and him is the object form.
panel.why: Subject and object pronouns.

teach.model: A pronoun stands in for a noun, like he, she or they. After a verb we use me, him, her or them. Adjectives like tall or red go before the noun.

points.ask: Which forms do I use after a verb?

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: How do you turn "You like tea" into a question?
explain: Questions often start with a question word: who, what, where, when, why, how. Yes/no questions use a helper verb first: "Do you like tea?" "Is she at home?"
Short answers are common: "Yes, I do." "No, she isn't." Use "Because..." to answer why questions.
stages.mnemonic: 5 Ws and H: who, what, where, when, why, how.

gq.q: Which is a correct yes/no question?
gq.why: We use do before you plus the base verb.

gq.q: "Why are you late?" Which answer fits?
o: In the park near my house.
gq.why: Why asks for a reason, so the answer starts with because.

panel.q: Which question word asks about a person?
panel.why: Who asks about people.

panel.q: Where does the question word go in "You live where?" in careful English?
o: At the start: Where do you live?
After the verb: You live where do?
panel.why: Standard questions put the wh-word first and use do-support.

panel.q: Why does English say "Do you like tea?" and not "Like you tea?"
panel.model: Modern English uses the helper do before the subject in yes/no questions.
panel.why: Do-support.

teach.model: Start a question with who, what, where, when, why or how. For yes or no questions put do or is first. Answer short, like Yes, I do.

points.ask: How do I ask yes or no?

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: Describe your best friend in three words. Which words did you pick?
explain: To describe a person, use adjectives with be: "She is tall." "He is friendly." For places say what is there: "There is a park near my house."
Use comparatives to compare: taller, more interesting, better. The word than follows: "My brother is taller than me."
stages.mnemonic: Short words add -er: taller. Long words use more: more beautiful.
sentences: There is a park near my house.
My brother is taller than me.

o: This city is bigger than that town.
This city is more big than that town.
This city is bigger that that town.
This city is big than that town.
gq.why: Short adjectives add -er and use than.

gq.q: Choose the correct word: "This book is ___ than that one."

panel.q: What is the comparative of "good"?
panel.why: Good has an irregular comparative: better.

panel.q: Which sentence uses "there is" correctly?
o: There is a river in the town.
There are a river in the town.
It have a river in the town.
Is a river in the town.
panel.why: There is is used with a single noun.

panel.q: Why do we say "the tallest girl" and not "the most tall girl"?
panel.model: Short adjectives form the superlative with -est instead of most.
panel.why: Superlative rule.

teach.model: Use is plus an adjective: She is tall. Use there is for places. To compare, add -er to short adjectives and say than.

points.ask: How do I talk about a place?
How do I compare two things?

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: What time do you wake up, and what day is it today?
explain: We tell the time with o'clock and past or to: "It is half past seven." Days of the week begin with a capital letter: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Daily routines use the present simple with time words: "I wake up at seven. I go to school at eight." Prepositions: at for time, on for days, in for months.
stages.mnemonic: AT the clock, ON the day, IN the month.
items: the first day of the week in many calendars
a day off at the end of the week

gq.q: Choose the right preposition: "The class is ___ Friday."

gq.why: Half past seven is thirty minutes after seven.

panel.q: Which is correct?
o: I get up at 6 in the morning.
I get up on 6 in the morning.
I get up in 6 at the morning.
I get up at 6 on the morning.
panel.why: At with clock time, in the morning.

panel.q: How do Americans usually write the date 3/4/2025?
panel.why: US format is month/day/year, while British is day/month/year.

panel.q: Why do we say "I go to school every day" and not "I am going to school every day"?
panel.model: Present simple is used for habits and routines.
panel.why: Habitual actions use the present simple.

teach.model: Say the time with o'clock, half past or quarter to. Use at for the time, on for days and in for months. Describe your routine with the present simple.

points.ask: How do I tell the time?
Which small words do I use?
How do I describe my day?

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: In a shop, how do you ask the price of an apple and say you want two?
explain: In shops we ask "How much is this?" for price and "How many?" for number. We say "I'd like two apples, please" to order politely.
Some nouns can be counted (apples, eggs) and some cannot (rice, water, milk). Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable ones. Use some in positive statements.
stages.mnemonic: Count the apples: many. Pour the milk: much.
items: a small white food from hens
a meal in the middle of the day

gq.q: Choose the right word: "How ___ water do you drink?"
gq.why: Water is uncountable, so use much.
We do not say two rices in standard use; rice is uncountable.

panel.q: Which is the most polite way to order?
o: Give me a coffee, please, now.
panel.why: I'd like with please is polite.

panel.q: What do people in the UK usually call fries?
panel.why: In UK English fries are called chips, while the thin crisp slices sold in bags are called crisps (in the US, chips).

panel.q: Why is "I have many money" wrong?
panel.model: Money is uncountable, so use much or a lot of.
panel.why: Countable and uncountable nouns.

teach.model: Ask How much? for the price and How many? for the number. Use I would like to order politely. Use much for things you cannot count, such as milk.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?
When do I use much or many?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: How do you start a conversation with someone new on a bus?
explain: A conversation has parts: greeting, questions, answers and a goodbye. Small talk topics are the weather, food and hobbies. "Nice day, isn't it?" is a typical start.
Use phrases to keep talking: "Really?", "That's interesting", "What about you?" Use "Excuse me" to get attention and "Sorry" for a mistake.
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?
It was nice talking to you.

gq.q: You step on someone's foot. What do you say?
Which is a good way to keep a conversation going?
gq.why: Asking a question returns the turn to the other person.

panel.q: When is "Excuse me" the better choice than "Sorry"?
o: To get attention or pass someone
panel.why: Excuse me is for attention or small interruptions, sorry for a mistake.

panel.q: Why do English speakers talk about the weather?
panel.model: It is an easy, safe topic that helps people start a friendly conversation.
panel.why: Small talk builds rapport.

panel.q: Which reply sounds most natural to "How's it going?"
panel.why: How's it going? is a casual greeting, not a question about travel.

teach.model: Start with hello, then ask a simple question. Listen to the answer and ask What about you? At the end say Nice talking to you.
